critique.good: Keeps the full endpoint path intact, preserves every method/auth/rate token, has no mid-word splits, and uses a one-line Rate limit header. Rows read as units and the 5-line descriptions are legible.
critique.problems: The table is 695px wide, overflowing the 360px box by 335px. At the phone viewport the first view shows only Endpoint and Method; Auth, Rate limit, and Description all require horizontal scrolling. Description still needs 5 lines, so the design pays a large horizontal cost without gaining compact rows.
critique.cause: Endpoint 282 + Method 76 + Auth 67 + Rate limit 89 = 514px before Description even starts. The 282px endpoint is irreducible, so overflow is structural. Description at 180px leaves only 159px for prose, which forces 5 lines.

critique.good: Narrower at 552px, so less horizontal overflow than r0A. Method, Auth, and Rate limit remain intact, and the table is visually compact horizontally.
critique.problems: The endpoint path breaks mid-word: '/api/v1/exports/{jobId}/download' becomes '{job' / 'Id}/download'. That destroys the row key. Description at 140px produces 7 lines and 176px rows, while Method/Auth/Rate limit cells sit in large empty vertical space. Rate limit's header also wraps.
critique.cause: Endpoint 190px is 71px below the 261px unbreakable path width, so the browser splits inside '{jobId}'. Description 140px leaves only 119px for text, producing 7 lines. The narrow endpoint and description create tall rows without solving the width problem.

critique.good: It fits entirely inside the 360px box with no horizontal scrolling. The first four columns are visible together, and the row order remains readable in principle.
critique.problems: The table is 2577px tall and nearly unreadable. Description becomes a 48px ribbon with about 5 characters per line; its header splits into 'De/scr/ipt/ion'. There are 61 mid-word splits, including endpoint fragments and prose words. Rows are 664–757px tall.
critique.cause: Endpoint 90px and Description 48px are far below their minimum unbreakable widths. The true no-split minimum is 282+76+67+78+106 = 609px, so 360px cannot hold this table without splitting words. r0C chooses splits everywhere to satisfy the box.

critique.good: Endpoint and Method both survive intact and on one line, headers never wrap, no mid-word splits, and Method/Auth/Rate limit sit shoulder-to-shoulder as a compact constraint block right after the row key. The endpoint path, which is the row's identity, is never mangled.
critique.problems: The box shows only Endpoint and Method (plus a clipped sliver of Auth); Rate limit and Description — the two columns a reader most needs after the route — are entirely off-screen. Worse, every row is 106px tall while the Endpoint cell holds a single 20px line: ~70px of dead white space under each path, repeated 4 times. The table reads as an empty grid with text pushed to the left edge.
critique.cause: Description got 221px (200px of text) so its prose wraps to 4 lines; those 4 lines set the row height for the whole row. Meanwhile the four left columns consume 282+76+67+89 = 514px before Description begins, so the table is 736px wide yet still starves the only column that needs width.

critique.good: Same strengths as r1A — intact endpoint, unwrapped headers, no word splits — and it is 70px narrower, so slightly less horizontal scroll.
critique.problems: Everything r1A does wrong, worse. Description at 151px becomes a 6-line ribbon of 3–4 words per line; rows balloon to 153px and the table to 578px tall. The endpoint column now has ~130px of blank space per row, so the visual weight of the table is white space rather than data. The reader scrolls right to find a description that is unreadable in a 130px measure anyway.
critique.cause: Trading 70px of table width away from Description cost 2 extra lines per row × 5 rows ≈ +160px of height. Description is the wrong column to squeeze: it is the only one with 670px of one-line content, so it is the only one whose width change moves row height at all.

critique.good: Keeps every endpoint path and all compact qualifiers intact. Description at 370px keeps long prose to roughly 2-3 lines, so the table is not excessively tall.
critique.problems: Still overflows by 525px. At 360px the reader sees only Endpoint and Method; Auth and Rate limit are off-screen, so the qualifier group cannot be compared. Row heights swing 36/83/60/36/60 because Description lengths wrap unevenly, so rows do not read as equal units.
critique.cause: Endpoint 282 + Method 76 + Auth 67 + Rate 89 already consume 514px, and Description 370 pushes the total to 885px. Description 370px gives 349px of text, wide enough for short prose to stay on one line but forcing long prose to three, creating the uneven rows.

critique.good: Narrower than r2A at 759px and reduces horizontal overflow to 399px; endpoint and qualifiers remain intact.
critique.problems: Description at 244px is too narrow: long rows become four lines, table height grows to 415px, and the one-line endpoint paths leave large blank areas beneath them. Rows feel tall and empty, breaking row-as-unit scanning. It still overflows by 399px.
critique.cause: Description 244px gives only 223px of text, so the 670px prose wraps to four lines. Endpoint remains 282px, so the extra height appears as dead space under short endpoint cells.

critique.good: All descriptions fit on one line, giving uniform 36px rows and very easy prose reading.
critique.problems: The 691px Description column dominates: total width 1206px, overflow 846px. Method, Auth and Rate limit are pushed far right; the first viewport shows only Endpoint and Method, so the compact constraints are effectively hidden. The reader must scroll a long way to connect a row's description with its endpoint.
critique.cause: Description 691px gives 670px of text, exactly the longest one-line width. With Endpoint 282, Method 76, Auth 67, Rate 89, the total is 1205px, so the one-line goal costs 846px of overflow.

understanding.purpose: A compact REST API reference table: readers find an endpoint, then check its method, auth requirement, rate limit, and description.
understanding.reading: Rows are read endpoint-first; the path is the row key, Method/Auth/Rate limit are quick qualifiers scanned across rows, and Description is read last as prose.
groups: Method, Auth, Rate limit: compact request constraints that belong together and are compared across rows
Endpoint: standalone row identifier and primary scan target
Description: free prose, secondary to route identification
keep_intact: full endpoint path and path parameters such as {jobId}
may_wrap: header labels such as Rate limit and Description
endpoint path only as a deliberate last resort when avoiding horizontal scroll

bad.why: Description is squeezed to 151px, producing 6-line cells and 153px rows; the table is still 666px wide, so it buys little horizontal relief at the cost of a 578px-tall, slow-scanning grid with large empty areas under Endpoint/Method/Auth.

Description is 691px wide (670px content), wider than the 360px viewport; after scrolling to Description the reader must scroll again within each line. The table is 1206px wide, over three viewports, for only one-line rows.
Endpoint is reduced to 216px, splitting the longest path mid-word; code identifiers must stay intact. The 136px width saving still leaves a 749px table that overflows by 389px.
Endpoint at 138px causes four mid-word splits, and the Rate limit header wraps; paths become hard to copy and scan, and the table still overflows by 300px.

final.rationale: The endpoint is the table's key and its longest path needs 282px, so it must not be split; Method, Auth and Rate limit are short categorical columns and should stay one-line. Description is the only flexible prose column: r2A gives it 349px of content, enough for a comfortable mobile measure and at most three lines, while keeping rows compact. The table still overflows horizontally because the first four columns alone are 514px, but r2A lets each description line be read within one 360px viewport after scrolling to it. Narrower designs add tall rows; wider designs force line-level horizontal scrolling.

general: Size identifier columns to the longest unbreakable token; never split URLs, paths, IDs or code tokens to save width.
Keep short categorical columns such as method, status, auth and rate on one line; their width is cheap and wrapping them hurts scanning.
For a prose column on a narrow screen, target a measure that fits the viewport once the reader has scrolled to that column, not the whole table width.
When a table cannot fit, compare total width against row height: over-wrapping prose creates tall rows with large empty areas in the left columns.
specific: This table cannot fit 360px: Endpoint + Method + Auth + Rate limit already require 514px, so horizontal scrolling is unavoidable.
Endpoint must be at least 282px to keep /api/v1/exports/{jobId}/download intact.
Description one-line needs 691px, which is too wide for mobile; about 370px gives 349px content and a 3-line maximum.
Method/Auth/Rate limit minima are 76/67/89px; extra width there buys no legibility.

final.tradeoffs: r3A is 70px narrower than r2A but adds 47px of height and two more 3-line rows; a designer prioritizing minimum total width could choose it. r1A/r2B are narrower still but accept 4-line description cells. r2C optimizes for one-line rows and desktop scanning at the cost of a 1206px table and description lines wider than the phone viewport.
final.uncertain: Exact wrap thresholds are approximate, and the row-height data show some variation that may depend on font metrics. If the publication target were desktop rather than phone, r2C or a wider description could be defensible; if horizontal scrolling were forbidden, no no-split design is viable.

A.why: Endpoint paths and methods stay intact, but the very tall rows leave large empty areas in the visible columns and make comparison slower.

B.why: Paths and methods remain intact, and the comparatively compact rows make the visible portion easy to scan. The remaining columns require horizontal scrolling.

C.why: Extremely tall rows separate the endpoints so far that comparison becomes difficult, with substantial empty space in the visible columns.

D.why: All columns fit in the viewport, but endpoint paths, headers, methods and description words split across lines. The resulting narrow columns make the table very difficult to read.

E.why: Intact paths and compact rows give the visible columns a clear rhythm, though the rest of the table requires horizontal scrolling.

F.why: Paths and methods remain intact, but the taller rows create more empty space than B or E and the remaining columns require horizontal scrolling.

reviews.unsure: The supplied images show only a sliver of the columns beyond Method in A, B, C, E and F. I cannot assess their widths, wrapping or full scrolling distance, so the ranking among those layouts is tentative.

A.why: Endpoint paths and methods remain intact, but most columns require horizontal scrolling. The visible rows have a reasonably steady rhythm.

B.why: Endpoint paths and methods are easy to scan, and the visible rows are relatively compact. The remaining columns require horizontal scrolling.

C.why: The intact paths are readable, but the tall rows leave large gaps between entries and make comparison slower. Most columns require scrolling.

D.why: Very tall rows create extensive empty space in the visible columns, making it difficult to scan endpoints together. Most columns require scrolling.

E.why: The paths and methods stay intact, although the visible rows are taller than in B and most columns require scrolling.

F.why: All columns fit in the viewport, but paths, method names, headers and description words split across lines. The resulting rows are extremely tall and hard to read.

reviews.unsure: The supplied views of A–E show only the endpoint and method columns and a sliver of the next column. The off-screen columns cannot be assessed, so B is a provisional choice based on the visible portion.

A.why: Endpoint identifiers stay on one line and Method is clean, but rows are ~120–140px tall with big empty bands under each endpoint, so the Description column is evidently squeezed into many short lines. Readable, but wasteful and slow to scan vertically.

B.why: Endpoint column comfortably fits the longest path (/api/v1/exports/{jobId}/download) with slack, Method sits in a narrow quiet column, and rows are compact (~75–80px), which implies Description gets enough width to wrap sensibly. Clear hierarchy, good rhythm; only the off-screen scroll is a cost.

C.why: Rows are ~250px tall with vast dead space beside each short endpoint — the Description column must be a narrow strip. The eye travels a long way between rows, and comparison across rows breaks down. Keeps identifiers intact, but the vertical proportion is badly wrong.

D.why: Only layout that fits 360px, but it pays with mid-word splits everywhere: 'Endpoi nt', 'Metho d', 'Descr i ption', '/api/v 1/user s/{id}', 'DELET E'. Descriptions collapse to 1–2 characters per line, so rows become unusable columns of letters and identifiers can't be read or copied reliably.

E.why: Much like B: full endpoints on one line, tight Method column, compact rows indicating a workable Description width. Column proportions read naturally and rows scan as units; cost is horizontal scrolling past Auth/Rate limit.

F.why: Same sound structure as B/E with compact rows and intact identifiers, but the Endpoint column is cut very close to the longest path, leaving almost no breathing room before the divider — slightly tighter and more fragile than B/E.

reviewsOld.unsure: The Description, Auth and Rate limit columns are off-screen in A/B/C/E/F, so I'm inferring their widths only from row heights; if one of them has an absurdly narrow Auth or Rate limit column that would lower its grade. Also debatable whether accepting horizontal scroll (B/E/F) beats fitting everything (D) — I judged scroll preferable because identifiers and headers stay intact.

A.why: Endpoint gets a comfortable full-width column so every URL stays on one line with margin; Method stays compact and the short columns are not inflated. Rows are only moderately tall, meaning Description (off-screen to the right) kept a workable measure, though the 360px view shows only Endpoint, Method and a sliver of Auth.

B.why: Very close to A: URLs intact, Method compact, rows a touch shorter than A so Description is slightly better served. Endpoint column is tighter than A's, leaving less safety margin around the longest path, but nothing breaks.

C.why: Endpoint and Method are given generous widths while Description is squeezed to roughly 15 characters per line, so rows balloon to ~185px and the table becomes a tall ribbon. Wastes vertical space on the two easiest columns instead of the reading column.

D.why: Method is padded to roughly twice its 55px content while Description is crushed to about 10 characters per line; each row is ~260px tall and only two and a half columns are visible. Proportions are inverted relative to content weight.

E.why: Short columns are kept tight and Description gets the largest share of the remaining width, giving the shortest rows of the overflow layouts. The longest endpoint just fits its column, so it works but with little margin.

F.why: Everything is forced into 360px: headers split ("Endpoi nt", "Descri ption"), URLs shred into fragments ("/api/v 1/user s/{id}"), and Description becomes a 10-character ribbon making the four-row table ~1300px tall. Identifiers are no longer scannable or copyable.

reviewsOld.unsure: Exact pixel widths are hard to read from the screenshots; A, B and E differ only marginally, and I could not verify precisely how much margin the longest endpoint (261px) has in B and E. If B/E's Endpoint column is under ~282px total, the longest path would be at risk of splitting, which would demote them below A.
